A single slow database query or API call can block the entire page. Streaming changes this by using [chunked transfer encoding](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Transfer-Encoding) to send parts of the response as they become ready. The browser starts rendering HTML while the server is still generating the rest. 18 19 This is especially impactful for pages that combine fast static content (headers, navigation, layout) with slower dynamic content (personalized data, analytics, recommendations). The static parts can be prerendered and served from a CDN, painting instantly, while the dynamic parts stream in from the server as they become ready. 20 21 React's server renderer produces HTML in chunks aligned with `` boundaries. Next.js integrates this into the App Router so streaming works without additional configuration. 22 23 ## Example 24 25 The companion [streaming demo](https://streaming-demo.labs.vercel.dev/) ([source](https://github.com/vercel-labs/streaming-demo)) lets you see each concept from this guide in action: 26 27 - Page-level streaming with `loading.tsx` (skeleton appears instantly, content streams in after ~2s) 28 - Granular streaming with sibling `` boundaries that resolve independently 29 - Hydration comparison: a single blocking pass vs split hydration with Suspense boundaries 30 - Raw HTML streaming in a Route Handler, with early CSS discovery 31 - A configurable `ReadableStream` API endpoint for experimenting with chunk sizes and browser buffering 32 33 ## How the App Router delivers a page 34 35 When a browser requests a page, two streams work together during the initial page load: 36 37 ### The HTML stream 38 39 React's server renderer produces progressive HTML chunks. The static parts of your page (layouts, navigation, Suspense fallbacks) render first and are sent immediately. You can prerender loading indicators such as skeletons and spinners, or a small but meaningful part of future screens such as a cover photo, title, etc. This helps users understand the app is responding and provides a better user experience. 51 52 Create a loading state by adding a `loading.js` file inside a folder. 53 54 61 62 ```tsx filename="app/dashboard/loading.tsx" switcher 63 export default function Loading() { 64 // You can add any UI inside Loading, including a Skeleton. 65 return 66 } 67 ``` 68 69 ```jsx filename="app/dashboard/loading.js" switcher 70 export default function Loading() { 71 // You can add any UI inside Loading, including a Skeleton. 72 return 73 } 74 ``` 75 76 In the same folder, `loading.js` will be nested inside `layout.js`. It does **not** wrap the `layout.js`, `template.js`, or `error.js` in the same segment. 87 88 > **Good to know**: If the layout accesses uncached or runtime data (e.g. `cookies()`, `headers()`, or uncached fetches), `loading.js` will not show a fallback for it. 89 > 90 > - **Without [Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/caching):** Navigation blocks until the layout finishes rendering. 91 > - **With [Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/caching):** Uncached or runtime data access in the layout must be explicitly wrapped in ``, otherwise Next.js guides you with a build-time error. Because the response headers have already been sent to the client, the status code of the response cannot be updated. 106 107 For example, when a 404 page is streamed to the client, Next.js includes a `` tag in the streamed HTML. This prevents search engines from indexing that URL even if the HTTP status is 200. See Google’s guidance on the [`robots` meta tag](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag). 108 109 Some crawlers may label these responses as “soft 404s”. In the streaming case, this does not lead to indexation because the page is explicitly marked `noindex` in the HTML. 110 111 If you need a 404 status, for compliance or analytics, ensure the resource exists before the response body is streamed, so that the server can set the HTTP status code. 112 113 You can run this check in [`proxy`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy) to rewrite missing slugs to a not-found route, or [produce a 404 response](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#producing-a-response). Keep proxy checks fast, and avoid fetching full content there. 114 115
116 When is the response body streamed? 117 118 The response body starts streaming when a Suspense fallback renders (for example, a `loading.tsx`) or when a Server Component suspends under a `Suspense` boundary. Place `notFound()` before those boundaries and before any `await` that may suspend. 119 120 To start streaming, the response headers must be set. This is why it is not possible to change the status code after streaming started. 121 122
123 124 ### Browser limits 125 126 [Some browsers](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=252413) buffer a streaming response. You may not see the streamed response until the response exceeds 1024 bytes. This typically only affects “hello world” applications, but not real applications. 127 128 ## Platform Support 129 130 | Deployment Option | Supported | 131 | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | 132 | [Node.js server](/docs/app/getting-started/deploying#nodejs-server) | Yes | 133 | [Docker container](/docs/app/getting-started/deploying#docker) | Yes | 134 | [Static export](/docs/app/getting-started/deploying#static-export) | No | 135 | [Adapters](/docs/app/getting-started/deploying#adapters) | Platform-specific | 136 137 Learn how to [configure streaming](/docs/app/guides/self-hosting#streaming-and-suspense) when self-hosting Next.js. 138 139 ## Examples 140 141 ### Streaming with Suspense 142 143 In addition to `loading.js`, you can also manually create Suspense Boundaries for your own UI components. The App Router supports streaming with [Suspense](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense). See the [Streaming guide](/docs/app/guides/streaming) for more on how streaming works, including granular Suspense patterns, Route Handler streaming, and infrastructure considerations. 144 145 `` works by wrapping a component that performs an asynchronous action (e.g. fetch data), showing fallback UI (e.g. skeleton, spinner) while it's happening, and then swapping in your component once the action completes. 146 147 ```tsx filename="app/dashboard/page.tsx" switcher 148 import { Suspense } from 'react' 149 import { PostFeed, Weather } from './Components' 150 151 export default function Posts() { 152 return ( 153
154 Loading feed...

}> 155 156 157 Loading weather...

161 ) 162 } 163 ``` 164 165 ```jsx filename="app/dashboard/page.js" switcher 166 import { Suspense } from 'react' 167 import { PostFeed, Weather } from './Components' 168 169 export default function Posts() { 170 return ( 171

179 ) 180 } 181 ``` 182 183 By using Suspense, you get the benefits of: 184 185 1. **Streaming Server Rendering** - Progressively rendering HTML from the server to the client. 186 2. **Selective Hydration** - React prioritizes what components to make interactive first based on user interaction. 187 188 For more Suspense examples and use cases, please see the [React Documentation](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense). 189 190 ## Version History 191 192 | Version | Changes | 193 | --------- | --------------------- | 194 | `v13.0.0` | `loading` introduced. | 195
